title: Lahaina Disaster Recovery Update Meeting: March 6, 2024

issues.title: Moving fire survivors off FEMA interim housing

recap.headline: Lahaina recovery update: mental health help, interim housing and Wahikuli water
recap.in_60_seconds: County, State, FEMA and Red Cross officials held a weekly Lahaina recovery meeting focused on mental health services and interim housing. Health staff described new wellness programs, crisis lines and a planned Resiliency Center. FEMA described the 169-unit Kīlohana group site, and the State described Kālai Ola, 450 units for FEMA-ineligible survivors, with first homes expected July to September. About 27 residents asked questions, mostly about Wahikuli water testing, expedited permits, being placed outside West Maui, and what happens when hotel sheltering ends April 10. The State has asked FEMA to extend hotel sheltering, but no decision was announced. Who will handle permits under a possible Lahaina community district was left open.

parts.title: Opening and announcements
parts.presenter: Meeting host, Mayor and West Maui Council member
presented: Host said about 200 Wahikuli residents attended an earlier Department of Health meeting on cesspools.
A homeowners meeting on infrastructure with County and State agencies is planned for early April.
Mayor said the temporary light on Keawe Street was changed to four minutes green and 20 seconds red.
The 450-unit State site will be called Kālai Ola and the 169-unit FEMA site Kīlohana.

next.when: early April, to be announced next week

parts.title: Mental health and wellness resources
parts.presenter: State Department of Health and Governor's Office of Wellness and Resilience staff
presented: Long-term stress can show up as anxiety, depression, sleep problems and other physical symptoms.
A federal SAMHSA grant will fund a Resiliency Center with therapy, peer support and traditional healing; its site and contents will be shaped with the community.
Free programs run at the Royal Lahaina and Kāʻanapali Beach Hotel; events are listed at mauirecovers.org.
Help lines: a warm line Monday to Friday 10 a.m. to 8 p.m., 988 for crisis, and a nearby behavioral health clinic.

next.what: Community meetings on what the Resiliency Center should include

parts.title: Interim housing overview
presented: About 4,500 households were displaced; 13% were homeowners.
More than 3,800 were sheltered in hotels at one point.
About 4,000 interim housing solutions are needed, from FEMA, the State, the County and private developers.

parts.title: FEMA Kīlohana group housing site
presented: FEMA has secured over 1,300 direct lease units and housed 378 households so far.
Kīlohana will have 169 units, mostly for single-person households, next to the State site.
Residents were urged to accept a matched unit even if it is not perfect.

next.what: FEMA housing at the resource fair at the Royal Lahaina

parts.title: State Kālai Ola housing project
parts.presenter: Deputy Director, State Department of Human Services
presented: Kālai Ola will have 450 units above the Villages of Leialiʻi.
Phase one is about 270 homes, placed July to September, then 180 more.
Studios to three-bedroom units from four manufacturers, with a post office, kūpuna gathering space and community spaces.

next.what: Kālai Ola phase one homes placed

parts.title: County projects, infrastructure and expedited permitting
presented: The County is speeding permits for private group housing, including a 50-unit project with a recent groundbreaking.
Sewer damage assessments are ongoing; the goal is to return residents to lots deemed safe.
An expedited permitting office is planned for next month, with neighborhood workshops in April.
Lots are hoped to be cleared, with some infrastructure in place, by early next year.

raised.concern: Whether Kālai Ola units will charge rent and whether they can be bought later.
Where Kālai Ola sewage will go, while nearby existing Wahikuli homes still lack sewer.
Construction and project traffic running through existing neighborhoods.
Whether the State units could be placed on survivors' own lots instead of a group site.
Mental health outreach has not listened to local helpers; residents already know their needs.
Whether first responders and teachers get priority, and an objection to any special preference.
People are leaving hotels with nowhere to go while businesses reopen before residents are housed.

answered.who: Deputy Director, State Department of Human Services
answered.said: Likely no rent in the first year, and any later rent would mainly cover utilities; units last 3 to 5 years, then may be sold at a reduced rate to move onto lots or go to Hawaiian Home Lands.

answered.who: Deputy Director, State Department of Human Services
answered.said: The project will connect to County water and sewer, built as permanent infrastructure.

answered.who: Deputy Director, State Department of Human Services
answered.said: Leialiʻi Parkway will be improved to two lanes each way; he will check with planners on other access.

answered.who: Deputy Director, State Department of Human Services
answered.said: The first 450 units go to FEMA-ineligible households in the group site; placing units on lots is a suggestion he will take to the Governor.

answered.who: Deputy Director, State Department of Human Services
answered.said: Early priorities include displaced kūpuna and families with children; first responders and teachers may be considered. All people are special, only 450 units exist now, and the Governor wants to build more.

answered.who: Deputy Director, State Department of Human Services
answered.said: No background check; people without ID can self-attest identity.

next.what: Kālai Ola eligibility and application process

parts.title: Wahikuli water update and questions
parts.presenter: Deputy Director, County Department of Water Supply
presented: Wahikuli remains under an unsafe water advisory; all mains are tested and results are pending.
Service lateral testing starts in 1 to 2 weeks; Ainakea Road could be cleared in 3 to 4 weeks.
About 1,800 laterals in zones L5 and L6 will be tested at about 200 a week.

raised.concern: Slow water clearance keeps standing Wahikuli homes empty and caused FEMA leases to be canceled.
Displaced tenants face obstacles moving into a new nearby complex, and it should be for fire survivors, not a lottery.
Confusion over whether water already declared safe is safe after EPA said it will test again.
Whether there is enough water for all the new units, including after 3 to 5 years.

answered.who: Deputy Director, County Department of Water Supply
answered.said: Testing follows a required protocol; Wahikuli could be cleared in about a month depending on what is found.
FEMA has no role in that complex or its lottery; it is a State question.

answered.who: Deputy Director, County Department of Water Supply
answered.said: If the County says water is safe, it is; he offered to check the address after the meeting.

answered.who: Deputy Director, County Department of Water Supply
answered.said: There is enough water to support the units on a temporary basis.

parts.title: Questions on permits, FEMA leases and sheltering

raised.concern: Who qualifies for expedited permitting, especially lots needing flood or historic permits, and whether building can start before infrastructure is ready.
Substandard streets and possible road widening or moving parcels affecting what owners can rebuild.
West Maui condo and vacation rental owners will not join FEMA leasing unless they can choose their tenant.
FEMA places families outside West Maui, far from jobs, while school bus service from South Maui is being suspended.
FEMA workers should treat survivors with more care.
Red Cross staff repeatedly ask hotel residents if they will move far away.
What happens between the hotel sheltering end date of April 10 and when interim housing opens.
SMA and State historic preservation reviews causing long delays, and rebuilding rules on the mākaʻi side and near the harbor.
Owners pulling out of FEMA leases, and whether they keep payments or can end a lease early.

answered.said: About 1,200 parcels will be eligible for expedited permitting, a map may show which; building before infrastructure is on the table, but procedures are not final.
The fire department did an initial road analysis; neighborhood meetings will cover what can be rebuilt. Moving parcels is a rumor, though road widening could affect some properties.

Federal fair housing rules prevent owners from choosing tenants under direct lease; owners can rent to someone they know using FEMA rental assistance. A contracting officer number was given to help find West Maui units.
FEMA has only four units in Lahaina; many West Maui homes wait on water and infrastructure. She will take the concern about staff treatment back to her team.
It is a standard intake question and should not be repeated once a person declines.
FEMA extended sheltering 60 days past February 10; any further extension is up to the Hawaiʻi Emergency Management Agency. The State has requested an extension, now under FEMA review.

A County archaeologist is working with State historic preservation on a faster review; homes under 7,500 square feet may qualify for expedited review; a Lahaina community district could make permits more complex.
Owners get only a security deposit until someone moves in; almost 300 owners have withdrawn; owners must honor signed contracts.
Households that do not qualify for FEMA are in one-year leases through a partnership with the Council for Native Hawaiian Advancement.

next.when: in a week or so, meetings start end of the month

parts.title: Closing remarks
parts.presenter: Office of the Mayor staff and Mayor
presented: Mayor's office staff asked FEMA and the State Department of Transportation to fund school bus service for West Maui students housed elsewhere.
Slides are posted at mauirecovers.org and on the County's Facebook page.
Mayor urged residents to follow up on mental health resources.

answered.said: Families housed outside West Maui rely on school transportation, so the service needs to be funded.

bills.name: Special Management Area permit
bills.what: A County permit required for building mākaʻi of the highway, which can trigger State historic preservation review.

open_questions.question: Will hotel sheltering be extended past April 10 until interim housing is ready?
Who will manage permits if a Lahaina community district takes effect?
Will there be enough water for Kālai Ola after 3 to 5 years if units are sold or go to Hawaiian Home Lands?
Why are displaced tenants having trouble moving into the new nearby complex, and will it use a lottery?

not_on_tracker.why: Standing homes cannot be lived in or leased to survivors until water is cleared.
FEMA-ineligible survivors need to know rent, eligibility and timing.
Owners need to know if their lot qualifies before starting a long permit process.

not_on_tracker.topic: School bus service for displaced students
not_on_tracker.why: Families placed outside West Maui cannot get children to Lahaina schools without it.
Residents are under long-term stress and want a say in what services are offered.

moments.quote: So the Kīlo Hana is a different one more towards the Kaiaulo o Fukuia development that's going on right now on the north side of Kiāwe Street.
moments.about: Explains where the Kīlohana FEMA group housing site sits and how it differs from the state's Kālai Ola project.

moments.quote: The group housing site is approximately 3,600 acres, 169 units. Majority of those units are for single households.
moments.about: Gives FEMA's early plan for Kīlohana as a 169-unit group housing site intended mainly for single-person households.

moments.quote: The comment period for environmental assessment will be announced on Friday, so that will be out for a seven-day comment period.
moments.about: Sets out the public comment window on the environmental assessment for the Kīlohana group housing site in March 2024.
